electronic structure and the periodic table

questions.q: In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing:
questions.explain: The modern table is ordered by atomic (proton) number. Mendeleev originally used atomic mass, which caused a few pairs to appear out of order.

questions.q: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same number of:
questions.explain: Elements in a group have the same number of outer-shell electrons, which is why they have similar chemical properties.

questions.q: What does the period number of an element tell you?
options: The number of occupied electron shells
questions.explain: The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells in the atom.

questions.lo: Mendeleev and the history of the table
questions.q: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his periodic table?
options: He predicted undiscovered elements would fill them
questions.explain: Mendeleev left gaps for elements not yet discovered and even predicted their properties, which were later confirmed.

questions.q: Where are the non-metals generally found in the periodic table?
questions.explain: Non-metals are found towards the top right of the table. Metals are on the left and centre; hydrogen (top left) is a non-metal exception.

questions.q: Which is a typical property of a metal?
options: Low melting point in every case
Good conductor of heat and electricity
questions.explain: Metals are typically good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable and often have high melting points.

questions.q: What is produced when a Group 1 metal reacts with water?
questions.explain: Group 1 metals react with water to give an alkaline metal hydroxide plus hydrogen gas, e.g. 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2.

questions.q: How does the reactivity of Group 1 metals change going down the group?
questions.explain: Reactivity increases down Group 1: the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost, so reactions are more vigorous.

questions.q: Compared with most metals, the alkali metals are:
questions.explain: Alkali metals are soft (can be cut with a knife) and have low densities - lithium, sodium and potassium float on water.

questions.q: At room temperature, chlorine, bromine and iodine are respectively:
questions.explain: Going down Group 7: chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid - melting and boiling points increase down the group.

questions.q: How does the reactivity of the halogens change going down Group 7?
questions.explain: Reactivity decreases down Group 7: the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so it is harder to attract an electron to complete the shell.

questions.q: Halogen molecules exist as:
questions.explain: Halogens exist as diatomic molecules such as Cl2, Br2 and I2 - two atoms sharing electrons.

questions.q: What happens when chlorine is added to potassium bromide solution?
options: Chlorine displaces bromine, forming potassium chloride and bromine
questions.explain: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2. The solution turns orange as bromine forms.

questions.q: Which reaction would NOT occur?
questions.explain: A less reactive halogen cannot displace a more reactive one. Iodine is below chlorine, so iodine cannot displace chlorine from KCl.

questions.q: Why are the Group 0 noble gases very unreactive?
options: They have full outer electron shells
questions.explain: Noble gases have full (stable) outer electron shells, so they have little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.

questions.q: Going down Group 0, the boiling points of the noble gases:
questions.explain: Boiling points increase down Group 0 as the atoms get larger, with stronger intermolecular forces to overcome.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic property of the transition metals?
questions.explain: Transition metals typically form coloured compounds, are good catalysts, and have high melting points and densities - unlike the reactive Group 1 metals.

questions.q: Compared with Group 1 metals, transition metals are generally:
questions.explain: Transition metals are denser, harder, stronger and much less reactive than the Group 1 alkali metals.

questions.lo: electronic structure and the periodic table
questions.q: An atom has electronic structure 2,8,8. Which group and type of element is it?
questions.explain: A full outer shell (8 electrons here) places it in Group 0 - a noble gas (this is argon).

questions.lo: electronic structure and the periodic table
questions.q: Potassium has electronic structure 2,8,8,1. This tells you it is in:
questions.explain: One outer electron means Group 1; four occupied shells means Period 4. Potassium is a Period 4 alkali metal.
